paras: The killing of Relford Pollard was the fatal shooting of a 34-year-old Black man by Richmond, Virginia, policeman W. J. Perkinson in a back yard on St. Peter Street on the evening of August 27, 1910. More than a thousand Black residents gathered after the shooting and were dispersed by police squads carrying riot guns. A coroner's jury and the Police Court exonerated Perkinson two days later, and the Richmond Planet denounced the shooting as an "unwarranted killing" and "useless slaughter."

According to the Times-Dispatch, Relford Pollard and his brother Thomas were fighting over a woman, Mazie Robinson, in a house at 1018 St. Peter Street in Jackson Ward when Policemen Perkinson and Guy Walker of the Second Police Station were sent to quell the row. The same paper reported, on their father's word, that Thomas had recently served a penitentiary term and that both brothers bore "a bad reputation."

In the police account, the officers heard a shot, broke open the door, and found the brothers fighting for a pistol; both men fled, Walker chasing Thomas and Perkinson chasing Relford. Witnesses at the inquest said Relford ignored two commands to halt and, when cornered in a yard, pulled a nail-studded rail or paling from a fence and struck Perkinson on the head and legs. Perkinson then fired, and Pollard ran, leaped a fence, and fell dead; Thomas escaped through the alleys.

Within minutes more than 1,000 Black residents filled the streets and alleys around the yard, and a caller warned the station of a feared clash. Squads armed with riot guns under Sergeant Neisz, Major Werner and Captain Epps reached St. Peter and Hickory Streets, where the crowd dispersed at their approach.

Sergeant Neisz swore out a warrant charging Perkinson with murder, and Judge Witt released him on $1,000 bond; Major Werner also suspended him. Thomas Pollard was arrested near the scene the next afternoon. Coroner William H. Taylor's autopsy led him to conclude that the policeman's bullet, which passed through the right lung and a large vessel of the heart, caused death.

On Monday, August 29, the coroner's jury sat nearly three hours and found that Perkinson had fired "in the discharge of his duty," and Justice John Crutchfield then discharged him as a case of self-defense or excusable homicide. Thomas Pollard was placed under $300 bond for twelve months after he reportedly threatened to kill Mazie Robinson, and Chief Louis Werner lifted Perkinson's suspension.

Richmond's white dailies told the story from the police side: the Times-Dispatch headlined "Riot Call After Officer Killed Vicious Negro" and "Perkinson Forced to Shoot," and called the gathered residents a "mob." The Richmond Virginian opened its inquest story with "Complete vindication" for the officer, while the Times-Dispatch remarked that acquittal was "a foregone conclusion" and that Perkinson smoked a cigar through the inquest with "complete nonchalance." Outside Richmond, the Washington Evening Star ran a special dispatch praising Perkinson as "one of the coolest men on the force," and the Mathews Journal carried both the shooting and the exoneration on September 8.

On September 3 the Richmond Planet reprinted the Times-Dispatch account, credited to that paper, and answered it editorially. Its editorial argued that the quarrel had been inside a house, that no warrant had been sworn out, and that Pollard could have been taken later, adding that if the policeman "had been a Negro and this man white" he would have gone to the penitentiary. A week later the Planet returned to the "unwarranted killing of Relford Pollard, (colored) by Police-officer W. J. Perkinson, (white)," writing that the inquest rested on the officer's statement because "the dead man could not speak" and that Black Richmonders were "in deadly fear of the Police Department."

The Washington Star named the dead man Thomas Pollard and said he had seized the officer's club after a pistol duel in the street, but the Richmond papers, which followed the case through the inquest, identified him as Relford and his brother Thomas as the man who escaped. Every account of the struggle came from the officers, and Thomas Pollard denied that any shot was fired in the house.

reader.title: Killing of Relford Pollard
bases: A Richmond policeman shot and killed a Black man he was pursuing to arrest; no mob took part in the killing, and the crowd that gathered was of Black residents (A2, A4, A13).

The Times-Dispatch, the Richmond Virginian, a Washington Star special dispatch, the Mathews Journal and the Richmond Planet all report that Policeman Perkinson shot Pollard dead on Aug 27, though the account of the struggle comes from the officers (A1, A2, A4, A11, A13).

accounts.label: Police account (Times-Dispatch, Virginian, Mathews Journal)
accounts.gist: Called to a row at 1018 St. Peter Street, the officers heard a shot, broke in, and found the brothers fighting over a pistol; Relford fled, tore a paling from a fence, struck Perkinson on the head and legs, and was shot.

accounts.label: Washington Star special dispatch
accounts.gist: Thomas Pollard had fought a pistol duel in the street with another Black man, seized the policeman's club, struck him on the head, and was shot.

accounts.label: Thomas Pollard
accounts.gist: After his arrest he said there had been no shooting in the house.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury and Police Justice
accounts.gist: The jury found Perkinson fired in the discharge of his duty; Justice Crutchfield ruled self-defense, excusable homicide.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet editorials
accounts.gist: The quarrel was inside a house and no warrant was out, so there was no need to arrest Pollard that night; a man fleeing without a felony meant no harm, and the inquest rested on the officer's word alone.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Riot Call After Officer Killed Vicious Negro' and 'Perkinson Forced to Shoot,' said both brothers 'bear a bad reputation,' and called the crowd a 'mob.'
The Richmond Virginian opened with 'Complete vindication' for the officer and set out the witnesses' self-defense account.
The Times-Dispatch's inquest story reported the exoneration but called the Police Court acquittal 'a foregone conclusion' and noted the officer's 'complete nonchalance' and cigar.
The Washington Star headlined 'Negro Resists Arrest, Is Shot by Policeman' and praised Perkinson as 'one of the coolest men on the force.'
The Mathews Journal headlined its exoneration story '[Poli]ceman Shot to Save Himself' and said Relford 'lay in wait' for the officer.

The Richmond Planet reprinted the Times-Dispatch story in full, then editorially called the killing 'unwarranted' and 'useless slaughter' and said a Black officer who killed a white man would go to the penitentiary.
